description: Simpson Manufacturing Co., Inc., together with its subsidiaries, designs, engineers, manufactures, and sells structural solutions for wood, concrete, and steel connections in the North America, Europe
description_full: Simpson Manufacturing Co., Inc., together with its subsidiaries, designs, engineers, manufactures, and sells structural solutions for wood, concrete, and steel connections in the North America, Europe, and the Asia Pacific. The company provides structural products for wood construction, such as connectors, fasteners, and lateral-force resisting systems; anchor, repair, protection and strengthening products including coatings, sealers, mortars, fiberglass and fiber-reinforced polymer systems and asphalt products. In addition, the company offers engineering and design services, as well as software solutions. It markets its products to the residential construction, industrial, commercial and infrastructure construction, remodeling and do-it-yourself markets. It offers engineering and design services. It serves its products to dealers, home centers, wood component manufacturers, OEM-relationships, distributors, and contractors industries. The company was founded in 1956 and is headquartered in Pleasanton, California.
ceo_bio: Mr. Michael L. Olosky | CEO, President & Director | Age 56 | Compensation: $2.4M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 5K people. Revenue per employee of $421K ranks in the below the sector median among Basic Materials peers, improving at 10%/yr — growing workforce leverage. Each employee generates $54K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $4K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 6× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (3/10).
financial_summary: Simpson Manufacturing Company,  is a mid-cap basic materials business with a $8.1B market cap on $2.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +3% over the past three years and +11% annually across the full decade, which puts it in mature, slow-growth territory.
Returns on capital run at 22% against a 10% cost of capital — a 12-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 45%.

The business throws off $298M in free cash flow — roughly 13 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.33× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.

Shareholder yield of 2.1% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insider ownership is negligible, so management has little personal stake in the long-term outcome.

sect: Its 20% operating margin runs 10pp above the Basic Materials median (10%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.

It accounts for 0.1% of sector revenue and 0.2% of sector operating profit.
Over five years it has been gaining share of the sector profit pool (+2.3% a year).
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.04 across 219 companies in the universe; the top four hold 25% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are roughly flat over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 8% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 29% and a beta of 1.00, it moves roughly with the market, though its beta has shifted (1y 0.27 vs 5y 1.00), so read it loosely.
About $50.2M trades a day, enough to build a position.
In past sell-offs it fell 44% in the 2020 crash, 43% in the 2022 bear market and 56% in 2008.
val: The price sits above its DCF fair value of $102 (margin of safety -92%), so there is no valuation cushion.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 34%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $84.15 to $127 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks expensive against Basic Materials peers: P/E 21.3 vs 16.5 and EV/EBITDA 13.4 vs 8.5 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 21% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are thin: an FCF yield of 3.7% (below the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 5.7% (vs the 8% bar).
The 5 covering analysts target $214 on average, 8% above the price, well away from the model's fair value.
prof: ROIC of 22% clears the cost of capital of 9.6% by 12pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 0.47).
It runs a 45% gross margin and converts 13% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.33x.
ROE of 17% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (1.5x equity multiplier).
It spends 1.0% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The balance sheet carries net cash of $84.1M (1% of market cap).
No distress or manipulation flags (Altman Z 7.1, in the safe zone).
Working capital ties up about 193 days of sales, a drag on cash generation.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 3.3% over 3 years, 13.0% over 5 years and 11.4% over 10 years, so growth is decelerating.
At current returns, reinvesting 68% of profits supports about 14.9% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 11.9% a year over five years.
Capex runs 1.8x depreciation (6.9% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 25, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 11.1% on average.
own: Insiders hold little stock (0.3%), and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
It returns 2.1% a year to shareholders (1.5% in buybacks and 0.6% in dividends).
The share count has shrunk 1.0% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
It has paid a dividend for 21 consecutive years, raising it 3.3% a year over the last five.
people: With about 5,545 employees, each generates about $421K of revenue, 0.7x the Basic Materials median, and productivity has risen 10.0% a year.
That works out to $54K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.4M (6x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (3/10, lower is better).
